intro: Next.js is powerful, but misuse of Client Components, caching, or routing can tank performance. Our nearshore Next.js developers operate with a server-first mental model, align to U.S. time zones, and keep Core Web Vitals within budget—validated by Axiom Cortex™.

pains.pain: Is your bundle massive and TTFB slow?
pains.problem: Overusing the 'use client' directive effectively turns a server-rendered app into a heavy SPA.
pains.solution: We ensure server-first composition and laser-focused client boundaries to minimize JS shipped to the browser.
pains.kpi: Server components usage and reduced bundle size

pains.pain: Confused by caching and revalidation rules?
pains.problem: Incorrect cache directives cause stale data or constant misses that hammer the backend.
pains.solution: We apply the correct mix of full-route cache, data cache, and on-demand revalidation via revalidatePath/revalidateTag.
pains.kpi: Cache hit rate and stable revalidation

pains.pain: Unclear when to use Server Actions vs API routes?
pains.problem: Choosing the wrong primitive leads to complexity and security risk.
pains.solution: We pick Server Actions for RPC-style mutations and Route Handlers for versioned REST APIs.

evaluation: App Router and advanced routing patterns
Server Components and data fetching strategies
technical_analysis: We evaluate Next.js developers with production-style performance triage. Candidates receive a mobile page with LCP above 4s and must justify server/client boundaries, select SSR or ISR with cache TTLs, and fix image and font loading. A strong solution from our nearshore Next.js developers replaces client-side data fetching with server components, implements next/image with responsive sizing, adds fetch(..., { next: { revalidate: 60 } }) where appropriate, and validates LCP < 2.0s and CLS ≈ 0 in lab runs. These nearshore Next.js developers must explain trade-offs (TTFB vs. cache staleness) and provide an observability plan to keep Core Web Vitals within budget under load.
